code.title: Surrogate PK plus UNIQUE natural key
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# surrogate PK (id) + UNIQUE NOT NULL natural key (email); nickname UNIQUE allows NULLs
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE users(
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,          -- surrogate key, invented
    email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,      -- natural candidate key
    nickname TEXT UNIQUE)""")        # plain UNIQUE: NULLs allowed
db.execute("INSERT INTO users(email, nickname) VALUES ('a@x.com', NULL)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO users(email, nickname) VALUES ('b@x.com', NULL)")
print("two NULL nicknames allowed:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users").fetchone()[0])
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO users(email) VALUES ('a@x.com')")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("duplicate natural key rejected:", e)
# the email can change, the surrogate id (and FKs pointing at it) stays stable
db.execute("UPDATE users SET email = 'a2@x.com' WHERE id = 1")
print(db.execute("SELECT id, email, nickname FROM users").fetchall())

followUps:
Use a natural key as the PK when it is truly stable, short and unique, and nobody will ever need to edit it. Good fits are ISO country codes ('IN', 'US'), currency codes or lookup-table codes. Bad fits are emails, phone numbers and names, because they change and every foreign key would have to change with them.

Natural keys also save a join: orders.country = 'IN' is readable without looking anything up.

Use BIGINT auto-increment when one database writes the rows; it is small (8 bytes), fast and keeps the index tidy. UUIDv4 is random, so inserts land all over the B-tree, causing page splits and a bigger index (16 bytes). UUIDv7 puts a timestamp first, so new keys are roughly ordered like auto-increment while still being globally unique.

Choose UUIDv7 when ids are made in many places (clients, services) or must not be guessable counters; otherwise BIGINT is simplest. Never expose a plain counter if enumeration matters.

code.title: ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL and RESTRICT

followUps:
In practice they behave the same for a simple delete: both refuse it while children exist. The difference is timing. RESTRICT checks immediately and cannot be deferred; NO ACTION checks at the end of the statement, and if the constraint is DEFERRABLE it can wait until commit.

Example: swapping two parent keys in one transaction works with a deferred NO ACTION constraint but fails with RESTRICT, because RESTRICT complains at the first moment a child is orphaned.

Delete in small batches, in child-to-parent order, one short transaction per batch, rather than one giant delete. A single huge delete holds locks for a long time and floods the log and replicas.

  1. Delete children in chunks of about 5,000 ids, committing each time.
  2. Pause briefly between chunks if replication lags.
  3. Delete the parent last, or mark it as deleted first.
DELETE FROM order_items WHERE id IN
 (SELECT id FROM order_items
  WHERE customer_id = 7 LIMIT 5000);

Repeat until 0 rows are affected. Each pass is short, so other queries keep running.

code.title: SQLite foreign keys off by default

followUps:
Because SQLite turns foreign keys on or off per connection, and the change is ignored once a transaction is open. SQLite changes this setting only when no transaction is active, since switching enforcement halfway through could leave data checked under two different sets of rules.

So run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON right after connecting, before BEGIN. If you ran it inside a transaction, read it back with PRAGMA foreign_keys;: it will still say 0.

First look at what the check reports: each row gives the child table, rowid, parent table and which FK failed. Then decide per case whether the child is junk or the parent is missing.

  1. If the child is meaningless, delete it.
  2. If it should be kept, set the FK to NULL (when nullable).
  3. If the parent was deleted by mistake, restore it.
DELETE FROM child WHERE pid IS NOT NULL
 AND pid NOT IN (SELECT id FROM parent);

Run PRAGMA foreign_key_check; again until it returns no rows, then turn enforcement on.

code.title: Add a NOT NULL column: expand, backfill, contract
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO users(name) VALUES (?)", [("u%d" % i,) for i in range(1, 11)])
# 1. expand: add nullable column (cheap, metadata only)
db.execute("ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN country TEXT")
# 2/3. backfill in small batches so each transaction is short
batch, done = 4, 0
while True:
    cur = db.execute("""UPDATE users SET country = 'US' WHERE id IN
        (SELECT id FROM users WHERE country IS NULL LIMIT ?)""", (batch,))
    db.commit()
    if cur.rowcount == 0:
        break
    done += cur.rowcount
    print("backfilled so far:", done)
# 4. verify
print("remaining NULLs:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE country IS NULL").fetchone()[0])
# 5. contract: SQLite needs a table rebuild to add NOT NULL
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users_new(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, country TEXT NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO users_new SELECT id, name, country FROM users;
DROP TABLE users; ALTER TABLE users_new RENAME TO users;
""")
print(db.execute("SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name='users'").fetchone()[0].split("\n")[0])

followUps:
A constant default is stored once in the catalog, so Postgres 11+ does not touch any row: old rows simply read that stored value when they are fetched. A volatile default such as random() or clock_timestamp() must give a different value per row, so Postgres has to rewrite the whole table.

Example: ADD COLUMN status text DEFAULT 'new' on 500 million rows is instant, while DEFAULT random() rewrites all 500 million under an exclusive lock. Note now() is stable within a transaction, so it is also fast.

Both tools copy the table in the background instead of altering it in place. They create a shadow copy with the new structure, copy rows over in small chunks, and keep it in sync with new changes, then swap the names in one quick step.

  • pt-online-schema-change uses triggers on the old table to mirror writes.
  • gh-ost reads the binary log instead, so it adds no trigger load and can be paused.

The cost is temporary extra disk space equal to the table size, plus a brief lock at the final rename.

code.title: Constraints in the database plus app validation
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE products(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  sku TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  qty INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (qty >= 0));   -- invariant lives in the database
""")

def app_validate(sku, qty):            # app check: friendly message early
    if qty < 0:
        return "Quantity cannot be negative"
    return None

def add(sku, qty, use_app_check):
    if use_app_check and app_validate(sku, qty):
        return "app: " + app_validate(sku, qty)
    try:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO products(sku, qty) VALUES (?, ?)", (sku, qty))
        return "ok"
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
        return "db: " + str(e)         # safety net for every other writer

print(add("A1", 5, True))
print(add("A2", -1, True))            # blocked by the app
print(add("A3", -1, False))           # a script that skips the app is still stopped
print(add("A1", 1, False))            # duplicate sku
print(db.execute("SELECT sku, qty FROM products").fetchall())

followUps:
A rule that looks like a fact but is really a business choice that may change: "customers get free shipping above 50 dollars". It reads like a constraint, yet marketing may change the threshold next week, and it depends on context (country, promotion, loyalty tier).

Compare with "quantity must be above 0", which can never legitimately be false. If breaking the rule later would be a policy decision rather than corrupt data, keep it in code or config. Another example: a limit of 5 addresses per customer is often policy, not an invariant.

Catch the database exception, look at which constraint failed, and translate it into a clear message with the right HTTP status. Give constraints stable names so the code can match on them instead of parsing text.

CONSTRAINT users_email_key UNIQUE (email)
-- code: if name == "users_email_key"
--   return 409, "Email already registered"

Use 409 for unique violations, 422 or 400 for CHECK violations, and 404 or 409 for missing parents. Never show raw SQL errors to users, but log them.

code.title: Small e-commerce schema with constraints

followUps:
Use a transaction that checks and updates stock in one atomic statement, so two buyers cannot both take the last unit. The simplest way is a conditional update that only succeeds when stock is enough.

UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1
WHERE id = 5 AND stock >= 1;
-- 1 row affected = got it, 0 = sold out

Backed up by CHECK (stock >= 0), so a bug cannot push it negative. With 1 unit left and two simultaneous buyers, the row lock makes the second update see stock 0 and affect 0 rows. For long checkouts, use a reservation row with an expiry time.

Split the product into a general product and its variants, and keep stock per variant per warehouse. The product holds what is shared (name, brand); the variant is the thing actually sold, with its own SKU.

  • products(id, name)
  • variants(id, product_id, sku UNIQUE, size, color)
  • warehouses(id, name)
  • stock(variant_id, warehouse_id, qty CHECK qty >= 0, PRIMARY KEY (variant_id, warehouse_id))

Order items then point at variant_id. Total available is a SUM(qty) over warehouses. Variable attributes can go in a small attribute table or JSON column.

code.title: Junction table for many-to-many
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE students(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE courses(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT);
CREATE TABLE enrollments(
  student_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES students(id),
  course_id  INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES courses(id),
  grade TEXT,                              -- attribute of the pair
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id));    -- no duplicate pairs
CREATE INDEX idx_enr_course ON enrollments(course_id);  -- reverse lookups
INSERT INTO students VALUES (1,'Ann'),(2,'Bob'),(3,'Cy');
INSERT INTO courses VALUES (10,'Math'),(20,'Art'),(30,'Bio');
INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10,'A'),(1,20,'B'),(2,10,'C'),(3,10,'A'),(3,20,'A');
""")
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO enrollments VALUES (1,10,'F')")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("duplicate pair rejected:", e)
# relational division: students enrolled in ALL of courses 10 and 20
rows = db.execute("""SELECT s.name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON e.student_id = s.id
  WHERE e.course_id IN (10, 20)
  GROUP BY s.id HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT e.course_id) = 2""").fetchall()
print("in both Math and Art:", rows)

followUps:
Give the junction table its own id when the same pair can happen more than once, or when other tables need to point at one specific row. Example: a student retakes a course, or a customer buys the same product twice. A composite key of (student_id, course_id) would block the second row.

Then add id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and put the distinguishing column in a unique rule, such as UNIQUE(student_id, course_id, term). Also use a surrogate when another table, like grade_appeals, needs a single-column foreign key to an enrollment.

Filter to the wanted courses, group by student, and keep only students whose count of distinct matched courses equals the number of courses wanted. This is called relational division.

SELECT student_id FROM enrollments
WHERE course_id IN (10, 20, 30)
GROUP BY student_id
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT course_id) = 3;

Example: if Ann has courses 10 and 20 only, her count is 2, not 3, so she is excluded. With the primary key (student_id, course_id) duplicates cannot exist, but DISTINCT is a cheap safeguard. Cost is one index scan over the matching rows.

code.title: DELETE, rollback and DROP
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:", isolation_level=None)  # manual transactions
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO t(v) VALUES (?)", [("a",), ("b",), ("c",)])

def count():
    return db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t").fetchone()[0]

print("start:", count())
db.execute("BEGIN")
db.execute("DELETE FROM t WHERE v = 'a'")        # DML with WHERE
print("after delete a:", count())
db.execute("ROLLBACK")
print("after rollback:", count())

db.execute("DELETE FROM t")                      # SQLite's TRUNCATE equivalent
print("after DELETE all:", count())

db.execute("BEGIN")
db.execute("DROP TABLE t")                       # structure is gone too
db.execute("ROLLBACK")                           # SQLite DDL is transactional
print("table back after rollback:",
      db.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE name='t'").fetchall())
db.execute("DROP TABLE t")
try:
    db.execute("SELECT * FROM t")
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    print("after DROP:", e)

followUps:
Because TRUNCATE does not visit rows one by one; it throws away the table's storage in one step, while DELETE removes each row and records each removal. On a table with 100 million rows, DELETE writes 100 million row-level log entries and fires triggers and FK checks, which can take hours.

TRUNCATE just deallocates the pages, writes very little log, and returns in seconds. The price: no WHERE clause, no row triggers, and restrictions when foreign keys point at the table.

It depends on the database. In PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite, DDL is transactional, so BEGIN; DROP TABLE t; ROLLBACK; brings the table back. In MySQL and Oracle, DDL commits implicitly, so the drop is final.

Never rely on this in production. Even where rollback works, the table is locked until you finish, and after a commit only a backup restores it. Take a backup or rename the table first (ALTER TABLE t RENAME TO t_old) and drop it after a quiet period.

code.title: Partial unique index: one default address
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE addresses(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL,
  street TEXT, is_default INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
-- only rows with is_default = 1 are indexed, so at most one per customer
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX one_default ON addresses(customer_id) WHERE is_default = 1;
INSERT INTO addresses(customer_id, street, is_default) VALUES (1,'A St',1),(1,'B St',0),(1,'C St',0);
""")
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO addresses(customer_id, street, is_default) VALUES (1,'D St',1)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("second default rejected:", e)
# switch default atomically: clear old, set new in one transaction
with db:
    db.execute("UPDATE addresses SET is_default = 0 WHERE customer_id = 1 AND is_default = 1")
    db.execute("UPDATE addresses SET is_default = 1 WHERE id = 2")
print(db.execute("SELECT id, street, is_default FROM addresses").fetchall())

followUps:
Do it in one transaction: clear the old default and set the new one, so the table is never left with zero or two defaults visible to others. With the partial unique index in place, order matters, because the old default must be cleared first or the second default would be rejected.

BEGIN;
UPDATE addresses SET is_default = 0
 WHERE customer_id = 1 AND is_default = 1;
UPDATE addresses SET is_default = 1 WHERE id = 42;
COMMIT;

If two requests race, one fails with a unique violation; catch it and retry.

MySQL 8 has no partial indexes, so use a generated column that is the customer id for default rows and NULL otherwise, then put a UNIQUE index on it. Since NULLs are distinct in a unique index, only the default rows compete.

ALTER TABLE addresses ADD default_cust INT
 GENERATED ALWAYS AS
 (IF(is_default = 1, customer_id, NULL)) STORED,
 ADD UNIQUE (default_cust);

Two defaults for customer 7 would both produce 7 and collide; non-default rows produce NULL and are ignored.

code.title: Trigger for non-overlapping bookings
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE bookings(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, room INTEGER, start_d TEXT, end_d TEXT,
  CHECK (start_d < end_d));
-- cross-row rule: no overlapping ranges for the same room (CHECK cannot see other rows)
CREATE TRIGGER no_overlap BEFORE INSERT ON bookings
WHEN EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM bookings b WHERE b.room = NEW.room
             AND b.start_d < NEW.end_d AND NEW.start_d < b.end_d)
BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'room already booked'); END;
""")
def book(room, s, e):
    try:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO bookings(room,start_d,end_d) VALUES (?,?,?)", (room, s, e))
        print("booked", room, s, e)
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as ex:
        print("rejected", room, s, e, "->", ex)
book(1, "2026-03-01", "2026-03-05")
book(1, "2026-03-04", "2026-03-08")   # overlaps
book(1, "2026-03-05", "2026-03-08")   # touching end is fine
book(2, "2026-03-04", "2026-03-08")   # other room

followUps:
Because the check and the insert are two separate steps, and two sessions can both pass the check before either one commits. Under READ COMMITTED each session only sees committed rows, so neither sees the other's new booking.

Example: A and B both book room 1 for 10:00 to 11:00. Both triggers run SELECT, find no overlap, and both inserts succeed, so the room is double-booked. Fixes: lock the room row first (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE), use SERIALIZABLE with retries, or better, an EXCLUDE constraint, which the engine enforces atomically.

In PostgreSQL, enable the btree_gist extension so integers can be used in a GiST index, then exclude rows with the same room and overlapping time ranges.

CREATE EXTENSION btree_gist;
ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT no_overlap
 EXCLUDE USING gist (
  room_id WITH =,
  tstzrange(start_at, end_at) WITH &&);

= means same room and && means the ranges overlap. Ranges are half-open [start, end), so back-to-back bookings are allowed. Insert conflicts raise an error at once, even under concurrency.

code.title: Cardinality and participation as constraints
code.python:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE departments(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT);
CREATE TABLE employees(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT,
  dept_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES departments(id));      -- 1-N, mandatory parent
CREATE TABLE badges(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  employee_id INTEGER UNIQUE REFERENCES employees(id));      -- 1-1 optional: FK + UNIQUE
INSERT INTO departments VALUES (1,'Eng');
INSERT INTO employees VALUES (1,'Ann',1),(2,'Bob',1);
INSERT INTO badges VALUES (1,1);
""")
for sql in ["INSERT INTO employees VALUES (3,'Cy',NULL)",   # mandatory violated
            "INSERT INTO employees VALUES (4,'Di',9)",      # parent missing
            "INSERT INTO badges VALUES (2,1)"]:             # second badge for Ann
    try:
        db.execute(sql)
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
        print(sql, "->", e)
print("employees without badge:",
      db.execute("SELECT name FROM employees WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT employee_id FROM badges)").fetchall())

followUps:
Put an FK on the side that is "many" and enforce the limit of two. Two ways: a junction table course_professors(course_id, professor_id) with a rule that each course has 1 or 2 rows, or two columns on the course.

courses(id, prof1_id NOT NULL REFERENCES profs,
        prof2_id NULL REFERENCES profs,
        CHECK (prof2_id IS NULL
               OR prof2_id <> prof1_id))

The two-column form enforces "at least one, at most two" declaratively. The junction form is more flexible but needs a trigger to cap the count at 2.

A weak entity cannot be identified by its own attributes; it exists only in relation to an owner entity. Example: an order_item line is meaningless without its order, and line number 1 appears in every order.

In SQL, its primary key includes the owner's key: PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no), with order_id a foreign key set to ON DELETE CASCADE. In ER diagrams it is drawn with a double border and an identifying relationship. A surrogate id is also fine in practice.

code.title: Exclusive arc instead of polymorphic association

followUps:
Rails and Django both have patterns for this, though they do not remove the integrity problem unless you add DB constraints. Rails offers belongs_to :commentable, polymorphic: true, which is the risky pattern. The safer ones are separate FK columns per target, or a shared parent via multi-table inheritance.

Django's GenericForeignKey is likewise unchecked by the database. Safer choices: one nullable FK per target with a CHECK constraint, or multi-table inheritance, where child tables share a base table and a real FK points to it.

Migrate in steps, keeping the old columns until everything works. First add the new nullable FK columns, then backfill them from the type and id, check for orphans, then enforce.

  1. Add post_id and photo_id (nullable).
  2. Backfill: UPDATE comments SET post_id = commentable_id WHERE commentable_type = 'Post'.
  3. Find orphans (ids with no parent) and fix or delete them.
  4. Add the FKs and the exactly-one CHECK, deploy code reading the new columns, then drop the old two.

code.title: Constraint test suite for a draft schema
code.python:
import sqlite3

# A tiny constraint test suite: each bad row must be rejected by the real engine.
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE COLLATE NOCASE);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0));
INSERT INTO users VALUES (1,'a@x.com');
""")
tests = [
    ("duplicate email, different case", "INSERT INTO users VALUES (2,'A@X.COM')"),
    ("order for missing user",          "INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,99,100)"),
    ("negative total",                  "INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,1,-5)"),
    ("order without user",              "INSERT INTO orders VALUES (1,NULL,5)"),
]
passed = 0
for name, sql in tests:
    try:
        db.execute(sql)
        print("FAIL (accepted):", name)
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
        print("ok (rejected):  ", name)
        passed += 1
print("%d/%d constraint tests passed" % (passed, len(tests)))

followUps:
The most common mistakes are the quiet ones: they work in a demo and fail in production. Typical ones are using FLOAT for money, forgetting NOT NULL, and putting no index on foreign keys. Others: blanket ON DELETE CASCADE, VARCHAR(255) everywhere, and timestamps without time zone.

They also forget case-insensitive UNIQUE on emails, mix dialects (using AUTO_INCREMENT in Postgres), and forget SQLite's FK pragma. Reviewing with a checklist and running constraint tests catches almost all of these.

Give the agent the least power it needs: a separate database user with read-only rights on a replica or a copy, never the production owner account. Limit it to approved schemas and views, and block DDL and writes.

  • Set a statement timeout and a row limit.
  • Log every query it runs.
  • For writes, make it propose SQL that a human approves, or call a small set of vetted functions.
  • Keep secrets out of its context.

Treat anything it reads as untrusted text that might contain instructions.
